newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian strongman Hun Sen capitalises on split.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian strongman Hun Sen capitalises on split.

text.p: Cambodian strongman Hun Sen has capitalised on a split in the ranks of his main rival's party in the ailing coalition government, but beleaguered First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh will fight to keep his leadership, analysts and officials said on Sunday.

Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's pledge on Saturday to give political and financial support to officials and members of parliament challenging the prince's leadership has fuelled tensions between his Cambodian People's Party (CPP) and Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC royalist party.

Hun Sen said the votes of 12 dissident FUNCINPEC MPs would give his party and its allies the outright parliamentary majority needed to pass laws but not the two-thirds essential to change the constitution, dismiss senior government officials and lift the immunity of MPs.
"You can be sure that CPP will take advantage of that majority," said a Western expert on the country's parliamentary affairs.

Hun Sen denied he was interfering in the affairs of FUNCINPEC, with which the CPP formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-run elections in 1993, but analysts said he was using the same strategy that divided other parties in the past two years.

FUNCINPEC on Friday expelled five senior officials, including dissident leaders Ung Phan and Toan Chhay, but has not yet taken action against the others. The dissidents have rejected Ranariddh's leadership and blamed him for the tense coalition relations.
Toan Chhay, governor of the northwest province of Siem Reap, has said the dissidents had formed an interim committee and would hold a congress to challenge co-Premier Ranariddh's authority.
Ranariddh and his supporters have made it clear they will fight back.
The prince still had veto power over government appointments and enough votes to prevent constitutional amendments and ministerial dismissals, a European diplomat said.
"It's like a wake up call, not just for Ranariddh, but also for FUNCINPEC," said a royalist party official.
But analysts said FUNCINPEC hopes, voiced by officials privately, of driving a wedge between Hun Sen and CPP leader Chea Sim, were naive.

Some analysts believed the developments of the past week would make all cooperation between the two parties impossible, noting that Monday's planned opening of the next three-month session of parliament had been postponed.

"I think the parliament does not work and the government also does not work. I think it is a big problem," said Kem Sokha, an MP of a rival wing of the Buddhist Liberal Democratic Party (BLDP), the third largest parliamentary party.
Hun Sen on Saturday warned Ranariddh against considering a pull out from parliament, saying: "If he withdrew his side from the national assembly it would be very bad luck for him."
A FUNCINPEC statement made it clear they believed Hun Sen had masterminded the split.
"This theatrical performance is fully fabricated and this drama is personally produced by Samdech Hun Sen...It is not an internal affair of FUNCINPEC," said the release.

Ties between co-Premiers Hun Sen and Prince Norodom Ranariddh have lurched from crisis to crisis since a deadly March 30 grenade attack killed up to 19 people at a demonstration led by opposition leader Sam Rainsy, an ally of the royalist FUNCINPEC party.

Tension has also been heightened by the unsuccessful attempt by former FUNCINPEC secretary general Prince Norodom Sirivudh to return home from exile to fight his 1996 conviction on charges linked to an alleged plot to assassinate Hun Sen.
